newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberians want African peacekeepers to stay longer.
newsitem.headline: Liberians want African peacekeepers to stay longer.

text.p: Ordinary Liberians and some political leaders are calling for the mandate of the regional peacekeeping force, ECOMOG, to be extended after elections planned for May in their war-ravaged West African nation.

West African foreign ministers concluded a two-day meeting in Monrovia at the weekend reaffairming that the Nigerian-led ECOMOG would start pulling out six months after a new government was installed.
But many Liberians interviewed on Sunday and Monday voiced concern over the planned withdrawal under accords that ended Liberia's seven-year civil war.
"We will ensure that ECOMOG leaves successors behind that will be Liberians," said Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi, who chaired the meeting of a regional committee on Liberia.
"There will be a new armed force and a new police force to carry out the duty of security and defence of the territorial integrity of this country," Ikimi added.
But Liberians, doubtful that their faction-ridden country can produce a neutral army or police in six months, are pressing the interim government to seek an extended peacekeeping mandate.

"We hope there will be a request to allow ECOMOG to stay far longer than six months because the new national army and police must be trained to become neutral," said former police commissioner Brownie Samukai.

"I would love to see ECOMOG here another year after a sucessful election," said univeristy lecturer Jeff Jallah. "It will take time for these new soldiers and policemen to understand their own role and duties."
Former guerrilla leader Charles Taylor who started civil war in 1989 has also come out in support of a longer stay for ECOMOG, a force he previously denounced as an occupation army.
In the early stages of the war, Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia battled ECOMOG troops sent to Liberia in 1990 by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS).
Now expecting to be elected president in May, Taylor argues there will be a security vacuum if ECOMOG leaves as planned.
"I have proposed to ECOWAS that following the elections the mandate of ECOMOG be changed and the mission extended," Taylor told Reuters in a recent interview.

"The new president of Liberia will havce to work with an extended mission because, by the end of the day, the army would not have been restructured, the police would not have been restructured," Taylor said.
"And ECOMOG cannot leave a void in Liberia. So I have proposed an extension by some 12 to 18 months," he said.
Ikimi said the nucleus of a new army and police would have been established by the time ECOMOG withdrew.
"By the time that ECOMOG departs, one brigade should have been established which will comprise three battalions. Similarly the police force will be established," Ikimi said.

The Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL), the former national army whose officers were largely U.S.-trained, disintegrated after then president Samuel Doe was killed at the height of the war in 1990. Doe's Krahn tribe dominated the army.
Surviving units of the AFL were disarmed by ECOMOG but a defence minister appointed under peace accords is projecting the force as the nucleus of a new army.

Meanwhile the United States military prepared on Monday to start airlifting troops from Mali, Ghana and Ivory Coast to reinforce the 10,000-strong ECOMOG ahead of the elections. U.S. military transport planes were standing by in Abidjan for the operation due to start on Tueasday.
Liberia was founded by freed American slaves in 1847 and continues to have strong links with the United States.
